title: Grumman F9F Panther
summary:
This document provides a comprehensive overview of the Grumman F9F Panther, an early carrier-based jet fighter developed by Grumman for the United States Navy, notable as the Navy's first jet fighter to see air-to-air combat and Grumman's first jet aircraft. The document covers the aircraft's design and development history, tracing its origins to late World War II jet engine studies, the G-75/G-79 design process, its initial Rolls-Royce Nene powerplant, distinctive design features such as permanently mounted wingtip fuel tanks, and its 1947 maiden flight and subsequent carrier certification. It also details the development of the swept-wing F9F Cougar derivative and Australia's brief evaluation of the type.

The operational history section describes the Panther's extensive Korean War service as the primary Navy and Marine Corps jet fighter and ground-attack aircraft, including the first U.S. Navy air victory of the conflict, claims of seven MiG-15 shootdowns, and a detailed account of a secret 1952 dogfight between Lt Royce Williams and Soviet MiG-15s. The document also covers the Panther's role with the Blue Angels, its service with notable pilots including Neil Armstrong, John Glenn, and Ted Williams, and its use by Argentina—the sole export customer—including its combat role in the 1963 Argentine Navy Revolt and withdrawal in 1969.

Additional sections include a complete listing of the aircraft's variants (from XF9F-1 through F9F-5KD), its operators, a catalog of surviving airframes on display or under restoration in Argentina and the United States, detailed technical specifications for the F9F-5 variant, notable film appearances (including The Bridges at Toko-Ri and The Hunt for Red October), and concluding reference materials, bibliography, and external resources.
